text: okay this is my problem statement

summary: Reviewed the supplied Track 3 brief and existing repository. Confirmed the repo is currently a minimal shell with no product implementation; defined the likely MVP around pre-render feed filtering, user semantic preferences, toxicity/NSFW warnings, and pre-post checking.

Read HANDOFF.md and incorporated its project state, decisions, blockers, and next priorities. Confirmed tooling is ready, application work has not started, and the agreed priority is a smallest reliable browser-extension-to-inference-to-filtering demo.

Evaluated the first objective, toxicity classification. Recommended unitary/toxic-bert as the initial server-side baseline because it is an Apache-2.0, multi-label BERT classifier with toxicity-related labels and Transformers support; noted its roughly 438 MB weights make backend inference more practical than direct browser execution. Recommended later ONNX export/quantization and team fine-tuning/evaluation before claiming metrics.

Confirmed that unitary/toxic-bert can be downloaded and run locally. Recommended downloading it into a local models directory or Hugging Face cache, serving inference from the backend, and excluding model weights from Git.

Verified the downloaded local model. models/toxic-bert contains config, tokenizer files, model.safetensors, pytorch_model.bin, Flax weights, README, and Hugging Face cache metadata; the model is available for local inference.

Confirmed the inference direction will use local PyTorch weights explicitly via AutoModelForSequenceClassification with local_files_only and use_safetensors=False. The toxicity model will be treated as multi-label and decoded with sigmoid scores.

Updated notebooks/01_toxicity_finetuning.ipynb with a valid seven-cell PyTorch notebook: local toxic-bert loading from pytorch_model.bin, multi-label sigmoid scoring, show/warn/hide classification, sample cases, CSV validation, and an optional Hugging Face Trainer fine-tuning/evaluation scaffold. Verified notebook JSON parses successfully.

Located compatible fine-tuning data sources. Recommended the Hugging Face google/jigsaw_toxicity_pred dataset because its documented schema matches the notebook exactly: comment_text plus toxic, severe_toxic, obscene, threat, insult, and identity_hate. Also identified the official Kaggle Jigsaw competition download as an equivalent manual-download option.

Diagnosed the dataset download failure: Hugging Face datasets rejected the google/jigsaw_toxicity_pred Python loading script because current Datasets versions no longer support dataset scripts, and verified data/toxicity/train.csv was not created. Identified a Parquet-backed Hugging Face mirror with the exact six-label schema as the compatible replacement.

Verified the fine-tuning dataset is present at data/toxicity/train.csv, approximately 68.6 MB, and its columns match the notebook requirements: comment_text plus toxic, severe_toxic, obscene, threat, insult, and identity_hate.

Confirmed CUDA inference works and patched the notebook's TrainingArguments construction to support both Transformers APIs by selecting eval_strategy or evaluation_strategy via signature inspection. The prior error was not a model or dataset failure.

Inspected the notebook's latest saved output. The current error is ValueError: expected sequence of length 130 at dim 1 (got 32), caused by variable-length tokenized examples being stacked by the Trainer without dynamic padding.
Patched the toxicity fine-tuning notebook to import DataCollatorWithPadding, create a dynamic-padding data collator, and pass it into Trainer. This addresses the variable-length batch ValueError.

Diagnosed and fixed the next fine-tuning error: DataCollatorWithPadding was treating the multi-label six-value labels vector incorrectly. Added ToxicityCollator to dynamically pad input sequences and stack float32 label vectors separately.

Planned the next work sequence while toxicity fine-tuning runs: finish and record toxicity evaluation, define a shared analysis response contract, integrate text inference into the backend, then add NSFW image detection. Identified Falconsai/nsfw_image_detection as the likely next image model candidate (Apache-2.0, normal/nsfw labels, about 343 MB), while using toxic-bert's obscene score as an interim text-explicit signal.

Addressed the long toxicity training time. Recommended a fast baseline for the hackathon: one epoch, a stratified 30k-row subset, max_length 128, larger CUDA batch size where memory allows, and fp16 mixed precision. The full dataset can be used later after the end-to-end demo works.

Explained that Colab GPU training may be faster than local training depending on the assigned GPU and local CUDA hardware. Provided a comparison-first workflow and noted the need to transfer model/data and save checkpoints because Colab sessions are temporary.

Compared the user's RTX 4060 Laptop GPU with likely free Colab hardware. Recommended staying local initially because the 4060 Laptop is likely competitive with a T4, and identified the notebook's on-the-fly tokenization in Dataset.__getitem__ as a likely bottleneck. Suggested fp16, larger batch size, shorter sequence length, and pre-tokenizing the dataset.

Optimized toxicity fine-tuning notebook after deciding to stop the slow run: samples at most 30k rows, pre-tokenizes all texts once at max_length 128, uses one epoch, batch sizes 16/32, and enables fp16 when CUDA is available. Notebook JSON remains valid.

Explained quality tradeoffs of the faster fine-tuning configuration: pre-tokenization does not change quality, while fewer examples, one epoch, and max_length 128 can reduce coverage or truncate long comments. Recommended using the fast run as a baseline and scaling to the full dataset after measuring validation metrics.

Adjusted the fast toxicity fine-tuning configuration for a quality/speed balance: increased max_length from 128 to 192 and num_train_epochs from 1 to 2 while retaining pre-tokenization and the 30k-row subset.

Compared Kaggle accelerators with the user's RTX 4060 Laptop. Kaggle documents P100 and T4/T4x2 options, with T4x2 available and P100 retirement announced for September 15, 2026. Concluded Kaggle is not automatically faster; a single Kaggle GPU may be comparable or slower, while T4x2 can win only if multi-GPU training is configured.

Verified toxicity fine-tuning completed. The fine-tuned checkpoint exists under models/toxic-bert-finetuned with model.safetensors, config, tokenizer files, and checkpoints. Saved validation metrics were eval_loss 0.02495, macro_f1 0.76456, and macro_roc_auc 0.99623.

Selected Falconsai/nsfw_image_detection for the NSFW image-filtering objective. It provides a PyTorch-compatible normal/nsfw image classifier; plan is to download it locally under models/nsfw-image-detection, verify inference, then create a dedicated notebook and integrate its score into the shared filtering response.
Repeated the NSFW image model download command for models/nsfw-image-detection.

Diagnosed the NSFW model download failure as a missing huggingface-cli executable on PATH. Replaced the CLI approach with huggingface_hub.snapshot_download via Python, which avoids PATH issues on Windows.

Verified the NSFW model files and created notebooks/02_nsfw_image_detection.ipynb. The notebook loads local PyTorch weights, preprocesses RGB images, computes normal/nsfw softmax scores, and returns a show/blur action with a configurable threshold.

Diagnosed the NSFW notebook kernel crash from the pasted VS Code log as Windows OpenMP duplicate runtime initialization (OMP Error #15, libiomp5md.dll), not a model or CUDA failure. Added KMP_DUPLICATE_LIB_OK=TRUE before PyTorch imports in the NSFW notebook as a practical Conda workaround and verified notebook JSON.

Recommended not fine-tuning the NSFW model immediately. First establish pretrained inference on safe and NSFW validation images, calibrate the blur threshold, and integrate image/text scores into the end-to-end demo. Fine-tuning should follow only if a suitable labeled image dataset and measured baseline weaknesses justify it.

Clarified that Falconsai/nsfw_image_detection exposes only normal/nsfw labels and should not be treated as a reliable gore detector. Recommended documenting it as sexual/NSFW detection and adding a separate violence/gore classifier only if the demo needs that coverage.

Selected sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for the semantic trigger filter. It is an English Apache-2.0 sentence-embedding model with local PyTorch support and roughly 91 MB weights, suitable for comparing user-defined avoidance topics with incoming post text.

Refined the semantic filtering design around a structured post object: combine title, caption, alt text/OCR, and account name into text for MiniLM embedding similarity, with lower weight for account names to reduce false positives. Noted that raw image pixels require a separate vision-text model such as CLIP or image caption/OCR preprocessing; MiniLM alone cannot embed images.

Specified the minimal dependency setup for the semantic trigger filter: install sentence-transformers in the active Jupyter kernel environment, with no OCR package yet. Recommended adding EasyOCR/OpenCV only when implementing image text extraction, since the first version uses title, caption, account name, and alt text.

Confirmed the semantic embedding package and model can be installed locally. Recommended using the exact Anaconda Python executable shown by the Jupyter logs so the notebook kernel sees the installation, then downloading the model to models/semantic-filter.

Confirmed semantic embedding model download completed, but identified a path issue: the command ran from C:\\Users\\Abhid, so relative models/semantic-filter was created outside the Warden repo. Recommended rerunning snapshot_download with the absolute Warden model path; HF cache should avoid a full redownload.

Provided the concrete path fix: change PowerShell directory to the Warden root before rerunning the semantic model snapshot download, or use an absolute Warden local_dir. Clarified that the existing outside-repo copy can remain temporarily.

Verified the semantic embedding model is in the Warden repository and created notebooks/03_semantic_trigger_filter.ipynb. The notebook loads the local MiniLM model, combines title/caption/alt text/account fields, computes normalized cosine similarity against a user preference, and returns a show/hide action.

Adjusted the semantic trigger notebook's provisional demo threshold from 0.55 to 0.40 so the tested war-related post with similarity 0.4046 is hidden. Documented that 0.40 is not a measured final threshold and requires calibration with labeled relevant/irrelevant posts.

Inspected the new semantic-filter example: the exams/studying post scored 0.3868 and was shown at threshold 0.40. Lowered the provisional demo threshold to 0.35 so it will be hidden, while retaining the warning that this threshold needs calibration.

For the fourth objective, selected local google/flan-t5-small as an offline text rewriter candidate alongside the fine-tuned toxicity classifier. FLAN-T5 is Apache-2.0 and supports text2text generation; recommended the small checkpoint for laptop inference and a prompt-constrained rewrite, with toxicity rescoring to verify the rewrite.
